title: Hydro-electric machines and powerhouse
summary: The turbine selection table is the most examined item in the whole chapter: Pelton for high head and low discharge, Francis for medium, Kaplan for low head and high discharge, with specific speed as the single parameter that decides. Two results are worth deriving rather than memorising — a Pelton reaches maximum efficiency at a bucket speed of half the jet velocity, and a reaction turbine needs a draft tube while an impulse turbine does not. Cavitation and runaway speed complete the subchapter.

sections.heading: Classification of turbines
sections.body:
**Two fundamental families**, distinguished by how the energy is converted:

| | **IMPULSE turbine** | **REACTION turbine** |
|---|---|---|
| Energy at the runner | **All KINETIC** — the pressure has already been converted to velocity in the nozzle | **Both pressure and kinetic** — pressure continues to fall through the runner |
| Pressure at the runner | **Atmospheric** throughout | **Above atmospheric at inlet, below at outlet** |
| Flow | Strikes only **some** buckets at any instant | Fills the **whole** runner passage |
| **Casing** | Not pressure-retaining — merely encloses | **Pressure casing (spiral/scroll) required** |
| **DRAFT TUBE** | **NOT required** — discharges to atmosphere | **ESSENTIAL** |
| Examples | **Pelton**, Turgo, **Cross-flow (Banki-Mitchell)** | **Francis**, **Kaplan**, propeller, Deriaz, bulb |
| Suits | **High head, low discharge** | **Medium to low head, higher discharge** |

**The draft tube distinction is the one examined most often**, and the reason follows from the pressure condition: an **impulse** turbine has already converted all the head to velocity before the runner and discharges **freely to the atmosphere**, so there is nothing left to recover. A **reaction** turbine's water leaves the runner still possessing **pressure and kinetic energy**, and the draft tube exists to **recover it**.

**Turbine selection — the table to memorise:**

| Turbine | Head | Discharge | Specific speed N_s |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Pelton** | **HIGH — above about 250 m** (up to 1800 m) | **Low** | **8 – 30** (single jet) |
| Turgo | 30 – 300 m | Moderate | 30 – 70 |
| **Cross-flow (Banki-Mitchell)** | 5 – 100 m | Low–moderate | 20 – 80 |
| **Francis** | **MEDIUM — 30 to 350 m** | Moderate | **60 – 300** |
| **Kaplan / propeller** | **LOW — below about 60 m** | **HIGH** | **300 – 1000** |
| Bulb, tubular | Very low (< 15 m) | Very high | > 800 |

> **LOW specific speed = HIGH head.** The relation is inverse, and getting its direction right settles many questions.

**Most Nepali plants use Pelton or Francis turbines**, because the terrain provides high heads. Kaplan turbines appear only on low-head schemes in the Terai and on some canal-based plants.

**Specific speed** — note carefully that the definition **differs between turbines and pumps**:

> **Turbine: N_s = N √P / H^{5/4}**  (uses **POWER**)
> **Pump: N_s = N √Q / H^{3/4}**  (uses **DISCHARGE**)

Using the pump formula for a turbine, or vice versa, is a standard error. Specific speed is the **speed at which a geometrically similar machine would run to produce unit power under unit head**, and it is the single parameter that identifies the machine **type** — which is why two machines of the same specific speed are geometrically similar however different their size.

**Why specific speed determines the type**, physically: a **high head with a small flow** must be handled by a machine that extracts a large energy per unit mass from a small mass flow — which means a **small-diameter runner with buckets struck by a concentrated jet** (Pelton). A **low head with a large flow** must pass a large mass through with a small energy extraction each — which means a **large-diameter, open, axial-flow runner** (Kaplan). Francis lies between, with a mixed radial-axial flow.

**Other classifications:**

| Basis | Types |
|---|---|
| **Direction of flow** | **Tangential** (Pelton), **radial** (old Francis), **mixed** (modern Francis), **axial** (Kaplan) |
| **Head** | High, medium, low |
| **Specific speed** | Low, medium, high |
| **Shaft position** | **Horizontal** (small units, Pelton), **vertical** (large units, Francis and Kaplan) |
| Blade adjustment | **Fixed** (propeller) or **adjustable** (Kaplan) |

sections.heading: Pelton wheel
sections.body:
**Arrangement.** The head is converted to a **high-velocity jet** in a nozzle, which strikes **split buckets** on the periphery of the wheel. The **spear (needle) valve** in the nozzle regulates the flow.

**Jet velocity:**

> **V = C_v √(2 g H)**,  with **C_v ≈ 0.98**

So at a 400 m head the jet velocity is about **86 m/s** — which is why Pelton buckets suffer so severely from abrasive sediment, wear rising roughly with the **cube** of velocity.

**Why the bucket is SPLIT and turns the jet through nearly 180°:**

From the momentum equation, the force on a vane turning a jet through angle θ is

> **F = ρ a V_rel² (1 + k cos θ)**

At **θ = 180°** the term (1 + cos 0°)... more precisely, reversing the jet gives **twice** the force of merely stopping it, because the momentum change is from +mV to −mV rather than to zero. So:

| Deflection | Force |
|---|---|
| Jet **stopped** (flat plate) | ρaV² |
| Jet **reversed** (180° vane) | **2ρaV²** |

**In practice the deflection is about 165°, not 180°**, and the reason is practical: a full 180° would send the returning jet **straight back into the oncoming jet and onto the following bucket**, interfering with it. The 15° offset lets the water leave sideways, clear of the wheel.

The **splitter ridge** divides the jet into two halves, each turned sideways in one half of the bucket — which balances the axial force on the wheel and lets the water escape cleanly.

**Maximum efficiency — the result worth deriving:**

The work rate is **F × u**, where u is the bucket speed. At **u = 0** the bucket does not move, so no work is done; at **u = V** there is no relative velocity, so no force and no work. The work rate therefore has a **maximum in between**, and differentiating gives

> **Maximum efficiency at u = V / 2**

**The bucket should move at HALF the jet velocity.** In practice the **speed ratio** is taken as **0.43 to 0.48** rather than exactly 0.5, allowing for friction and the finite number of buckets.

The corresponding theoretical hydraulic efficiency is

> **η = (1 + k cos θ)/2**

which for an ideal frictionless 180° bucket gives **100%**, and for realistic values about **85–90%**.

**Other Pelton parameters:**

| Parameter | Typical |
|---|---|
| **Number of buckets** | **Z = 15 + D/(2d)** (D wheel diameter, d jet diameter) — usually 17 to 26 |
| **Jet ratio m = D/d** | **11 to 14** typically |
| Number of jets | 1 to 6 (more jets allow a larger flow at the same wheel size) |
| Speed ratio | 0.43 – 0.48 |
| **Overall efficiency** | **85 – 90%** |

**Multiple jets** are the way a Pelton handles a larger flow without an impractically large wheel: up to six jets on a vertical-shaft machine, each with its own nozzle and needle. It also gives **part-load flexibility**, since jets can be shut off individually — and that is why the Pelton holds its efficiency well at part load, an important property for a run-of-river plant whose flow varies through the year.

**Regulation** is by the **spear (needle) valve**, moved by the governor. A **deflector plate** is provided to swing the jet away from the buckets for **emergency shutdown**, because closing the needle rapidly would cause water hammer in the penstock — so the jet is deflected first and the needle then closed slowly. That arrangement is a neat illustration of the coupling between the mechanical and civil designs.

sections.heading: Reaction turbines — Francis and Kaplan
sections.body:
**Components of a reaction turbine**, in the order water passes them:

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **Spiral (scroll) casing** | Distributes water **uniformly around the runner**; its area decreases so the velocity stays constant |
| **Stay ring / stay vanes** | Structural; guides the flow inward |
| **Guide vanes (wicket gates)** | **Adjustable** — regulate the discharge and direct the flow onto the runner at the correct angle |
| **Runner** | Extracts the energy |
| **Draft tube** | **Recovers the exit energy** and permits the runner to be set above tailwater |

**Francis turbine.** A **mixed-flow** machine: water enters **radially** at the periphery and leaves **axially** at the centre. (The original Francis was purely radial; all modern ones are mixed flow.)

| Parameter | Typical |
|---|---|
| Head | **30 – 350 m** |
| Specific speed | 60 – 300 |
| Flow ratio | 0.15 – 0.30 |
| Speed ratio | 0.6 – 0.9 |
| **Overall efficiency** | **90 – 95%** — the highest of any turbine at its design point |
| Part-load behaviour | **Efficiency falls appreciably** below about 50% of design flow |

**Francis turbines achieve the highest peak efficiency** but their **part-load performance is comparatively poor**, because the fixed runner blade angles no longer match the flow when the guide vanes are throttled. That matters for a Nepali run-of-river plant, whose flow varies greatly — which is why such schemes are often built with **two or three smaller units** rather than one large one, so that units can be shut down and the remainder run near their design point.

**Kaplan turbine.** An **axial-flow** propeller machine for **low head and high discharge**.

| Parameter | Typical |
|---|---|
| Head | **Below about 60 m** |
| Specific speed | 300 – 1000 |
| Number of blades | **3 to 8** — few, because the head is low |
| **Overall efficiency** | 90 – 94% |
| **Blades** | **ADJUSTABLE** |

**The Kaplan's adjustable blades are its defining feature**, and they solve exactly the problem Francis has: the blades rotate to match the flow as it varies, so the **efficiency stays high over a wide range of discharge**. A **propeller turbine** is the same machine with **fixed** blades — cheaper, but with a sharply peaked efficiency curve.

**Double regulation** is the term for a Kaplan's simultaneous adjustment of **guide vanes and runner blades**, coordinated by a cam so that each combination is the optimum for that flow. It is the reason a Kaplan can run efficiently from 30% to 100% of its design flow — a very valuable property where the flow is variable, which is why Kaplans dominate low-head river plants.

**The draft tube** — its two functions:

| Function | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **Recovers the exit kinetic energy** | By **gradually expanding**, it converts the runner's exit velocity head into a **pressure recovery**, which increases the effective head across the runner |
| **Permits the runner to be set above tailwater** | By creating a **partial vacuum** at the runner exit, so the head between the runner and the tailwater is not lost |

**The second function is the more important and the less obvious.** Without a draft tube, a reaction turbine would have to be set **at or below tailwater level** to use the full head — which is inconvenient and, for a large machine, expensive. The draft tube's suction lets the runner sit **above** the tailwater while still using the head down to it.

**Types of draft tube:**

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| **Conical (straight divergent)** | Simple; best efficiency (~90%); needs vertical depth |
| **Elbow** | Turns the flow to horizontal; **less excavation** — the standard for large vertical units |
| Moody spreading (hydracone) | Reduces swirl |
| Simple elbow with varying section | — |

The **elbow draft tube dominates practice** because it drastically reduces the depth of excavation below the powerhouse — a large cost item — at a modest efficiency penalty.

**Cavitation** is the characteristic hazard of reaction turbines:

> Where the local pressure falls to the **vapour pressure**, **vapour bubbles form**; carried into a higher-pressure region they **collapse violently**, and the repeated pressure pulses **pit and erode the metal**.

It occurs at the **runner outlet and on the blade suction surfaces**, where the pressure is lowest.

**Thoma's cavitation factor:**

> **σ = (H_atm − H_vapour − H_s) / H**

where **H_s** is the **suction head** — the height of the runner above the tailwater. Cavitation is avoided while **σ > σ_critical**, which is tabulated against specific speed.

**The design consequence:**

> The **runner SETTING LEVEL** relative to the tailwater is fixed by the cavitation criterion. A high specific speed machine (Kaplan) requires a **lower setting**, often **below tailwater level**.

So a Kaplan turbine is normally **submerged**, and that is a **cavitation requirement, not a convenience** — which is a favourite examination point. The higher the specific speed, the greater the required submergence.

**Note also the altitude effect**, which matters in Nepal: **H_atm falls with elevation**, so σ falls, so a turbine that is safe at sea level may cavitate at the same setting in a high valley. The setting must be computed with the **local** atmospheric pressure — about 8.6 m of water at 1400 m (Kathmandu) against 10.3 m at sea level.

**Consequences of cavitation:** **pitting and erosion** of blades, **loss of efficiency**, **vibration and noise**, and eventual **structural failure** of the blade. It is countered by adequate submergence, **cavitation-resistant materials** (stainless steel overlay), smooth blade profiles, and avoiding operation at part loads where the flow separates.

sections.heading: Generators, governing and the powerhouse
sections.body:
**Synchronous speed** — the relation that fixes the turbine speed:

> **N = 120 f / P**  (f = frequency in Hz, P = number of poles)

Nepal's grid frequency is **50 Hz**, so:

| Poles | Speed (rpm) |
|---|---|
| 4 | 1500 |
| **6** | **1000** |
| 8 | 750 |
| 12 | 500 |
| 24 | 250 |
| 48 | 125 |

**The turbine speed must equal a synchronous speed**, so the turbine can only be designed for a **discrete set of speeds**, not any value. That constraint feeds back into the runner design and diameter.

**A consequence worth noting:** a **high-head Pelton runs fast** (few poles, physically small generator), while a **low-head Kaplan runs slowly** (many poles, physically very large generator). That is why a low-head plant's generator is enormous relative to its output — the machine must be large in diameter to accommodate the poles, whatever its power.

**Generator basics:**

| Item | Note |
|---|---|
| Type | **Synchronous** alternator; salient pole for hydro (low speed) |
| Excitation | Static or brushless |
| Cooling | Air (small), or air/water heat exchanger (large) |
| **Power factor** | Typically **0.85 – 0.9** lagging |
| **Rating** | In **kVA** or MVA (apparent power); the turbine is rated in kW |
| Efficiency | 95 – 98% |

The **kVA/kW distinction** is worth holding: **kW = kVA × power factor**, so a generator rated 10 MVA at 0.85 pf delivers **8.5 MW**. Confusing the two overstates the plant's output.

**Governing** — and the reason it is essential rather than merely convenient:

> A **governor maintains constant turbine SPEED, and therefore constant grid FREQUENCY, irrespective of load variation.**

Because **f = NP/120**, frequency is directly proportional to speed. If the load falls and the turbine is not throttled, it **accelerates**, and the frequency rises; if the load rises and no more water is admitted, it **decelerates**. Since the whole grid must stay at **50 Hz** within a narrow tolerance, speed control is a **system stability requirement**.

**How the governor acts:**

| Turbine | Control element |
|---|---|
| **Pelton** | **Spear (needle) valve**, plus a **deflector** for emergency |
| **Francis** | **Guide vanes (wicket gates)** |
| **Kaplan** | **Guide vanes AND runner blades** (double regulation) |

**The governing chain:** a **speed sensor** detects the deviation → the **actuator (servomotor)** moves the control element → the discharge changes → the speed returns. Older machines used a **mechanical (centrifugal) governor**; modern ones use **electro-hydraulic** or **digital** governors with much better response.

**The conflict the governor must resolve** is worth understanding, because it links back to the civil design: **rapid closure gives good speed regulation but causes water hammer**; slow closure protects the penstock but allows the speed to overshoot. The resolution is a **surge tank or relief valve** (which permits faster closure safely), or a **flywheel** (which increases the rotating inertia so the speed changes more slowly for a given imbalance).

**Runaway speed** — the condition if the load is lost and the governor fails to act:

| Turbine | Runaway speed |
|---|---|
| **Pelton** | **1.8 × rated** |
| **Francis** | **2.0 × rated** |
| **Kaplan** | **2.5 – 3.0 × rated** |

> **The generator and all rotating parts must be designed to SURVIVE the runaway speed**, because centrifugal stress rises with the **square** of speed — so a Kaplan's rotor experiences up to **nine times** the normal centrifugal force.

That is a **mechanical design requirement independent of normal operating conditions**, and it is why a hydro generator's rotor is a substantial forging rather than sized for its duty alone.

**Powerhouse types:**

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| **Surface** | Conventional; cheapest where a safe site exists |
| **Semi-underground** | Partly excavated into the hillside |
| **Underground (cavern)** | Fully excavated; **protected from rockfall, landslide, avalanche and flood** |
| Shaft | The machine in a vertical shaft |

**Underground powerhouses are increasingly chosen in Nepal**, and the reasons are the site hazards rather than any hydraulic advantage: a surface powerhouse in a steep Himalayan valley is exposed to **rockfall, landslide, debris flow and flood**, and a **debris fan at a tributary mouth** — which looks like the only flat site available — is precisely the deposit of the event that would destroy the building. An underground cavern avoids all of it, at the cost of excavation and a long access tunnel.

**Powerhouse contents:**

| Equipment | Function |
|---|---|
| **Turbine and generator** | Generation |
| **Governor and its oil system** | Speed control |
| **Main inlet valve** | Isolation of the turbine |
| **Transformer** | Steps up to transmission voltage |
| **Switchgear and switchyard** | Protection and connection to the grid |
| **Control room** | Operation, protection, metering, SCADA |
| **EOT crane** | Erection and maintenance of the heavy machines |
| Auxiliary systems | Cooling water, drainage and dewatering, compressed air, station supply, battery, fire protection |
| **Erection bay** | Space to assemble and dismantle a unit |

**The EOT crane and erection bay govern the powerhouse dimensions**, which is the practical point: the building must be long enough to accommodate the units **plus an erection bay**, and tall enough for the crane to **lift a rotor clear of an adjacent machine**. Those clearances, not the machines themselves, usually set the size.

**Number of units.** A single large unit is cheaper per kW, but:

| Multiple units | Single unit |
|---|---|
| **Higher efficiency at part flow** — shut some down and run the rest near design point | Poor part-load efficiency |
| **Redundancy** — an outage does not stop generation | Total outage during maintenance |
| Easier transport of components to a remote site | Very heavy single pieces |
| Higher cost per kW | Lower |

**For a Nepali run-of-river plant the part-flow argument is usually decisive**: with the flow varying several-fold through the year, **two or three units** allow the plant to track the available flow while each running unit stays near its efficient point. The transport argument matters too — a runner that can be carried on the available roads is worth more than a marginally more efficient one that cannot reach the site.

formulas.label: Turbine selection by specific speed
formulas.expression: Pelton 8–30 (high head) ; Francis 60–300 (medium) ; Kaplan 300–1000 (low head, high discharge)
formulas.note: LOW specific speed = HIGH head. Most Nepali plants are Pelton or Francis.

formulas.label: Specific speed — turbine and pump differ
formulas.expression: Turbine: N_s = N√P/H^{5/4}   ·   Pump: N_s = N√Q/H^{3/4}
formulas.note: The turbine form uses POWER, the pump form DISCHARGE. Using the wrong one is a standard error.

formulas.label: Pelton jet velocity and optimum bucket speed
formulas.expression: V = C_v√(2gH), C_v ≈ 0.98 ;   maximum efficiency at u = V/2 (speed ratio 0.43–0.48)
formulas.note: Reversing the jet gives 2ρaV², twice the force of stopping it — hence the split bucket at about 165°.

formulas.label: Pelton geometry
formulas.expression: buckets Z = 15 + D/(2d) ;   jet ratio D/d = 11–14 ;   up to 6 jets
formulas.note: Multiple jets allow larger flow and give good part-load flexibility by shutting jets off individually.

formulas.label: Draft tube — the two functions
formulas.expression: Recovers the exit kinetic energy, AND permits the runner to be set above tailwater
formulas.note: Essential for a REACTION turbine; an impulse turbine has none, discharging to atmosphere.

formulas.label: Thoma's cavitation factor
formulas.expression: σ = (H_atm − H_vapour − H_s)/H,  and σ must exceed σ_critical
formulas.note: Fixes the runner SETTING level. High specific speed (Kaplan) requires submergence below tailwater.

formulas.label: Synchronous speed
formulas.expression: N = 120 f / P     (f = 50 Hz in Nepal)
formulas.note: 6 poles → 1000 rpm. High-head Pelton runs fast with few poles; low-head Kaplan slowly with many.

formulas.label: Runaway speed
formulas.note: All rotating parts must SURVIVE it. Centrifugal stress rises as the SQUARE of speed.

formulas.label: Generator rating
formulas.note: The generator is rated in kVA (apparent power), the turbine in kW.
